relations.subject: encryption:master-password
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - for audit/configuration/log data specifically, an administrator chooses between the master password and an encryption-at-rest key; bucket data has no such choice - see doesNotSupport note below
relations.evidence: You must use an encryption-at-rest key to encrypt bucket data. You can choose to use the [master password](manage-system-secrets.md#setting-the-master-password) instead of an encryption-at-rest key to encrypt audit, configuration, and log data.

relations.subject: encryption:native-encryption-at-rest
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - bucket-data encryption specifically has no master-password path, unlike audit/configuration/log data (see offersConfigurationChoice relation above)
relations.evidence: Couchbase Server only supports encrypting bucket data using an encryption at rest key.

relations.subject: encryption:encryption-at-rest-key
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - predicate minted in learn/security/native-encryption-at-rest-overview.json for the identical relation; this page corroborates it from the rotation procedure
relations.evidence: When you rotate an encryption-at-rest key, Couchbase Server creates a new key and uses it to re-encrypt all DEKs that were encrypted with the previous version of the key. This process does not re-encrypt data, as the DEKs do not change.

relations.subject: kms:aws-kms
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - AWS-managed keys cannot be rotated through Couchbase Server's own rotation action at all, only through AWS's own tools, after which Couchbase Server must be told to re-encrypt DEKs separately
relations.evidence: To rotate an encryption-at-rest key managed by an external KMS, you must use the KMS's tools to rotate the key, then have Couchbase Server re-encrypt DEKs with the new key.

relations.subject: encryption:drop-deks-rest-action
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the page states this disambiguation explicitly and by name, the strongest kind of licence this predicate requires
relations.evidence: Dropping DEKs is not the same as rotating DEKs. When Couchbase Server automatically rotates a DEK, it makes it inactive, creates a new active DEK, and then uses that for newly written data. It does not re-encrypt data, nor does it immediately remove the old DEKs.

relations.subject: encryption:drop-deks-rest-action
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - dropping DEKs for a bucket/data-type replaces every DEK for it and re-encrypts all affected data, then deletes the old DEKs
relations.evidence: When you drop the DEKs for a bucket or type of data, Couchbase Server creates a new replacement DEK and uses it to re-encrypt all of the data in the bucket or of that type. Then it removes the old DEKs.

relations.subject: kms:kmip-kms
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - a KMIP- or AWS-managed key cannot directly encrypt data at all; it may only be configured as a Key Encryption Key protecting a Couchbase-Server-managed key, which is what actually does the data encryption
relations.evidence: If you're creating an encryption key managed by a KMIP KMS or AWS KMS, only leave **Key Encryption Key (KEK)** selected. Then use the key to encrypt an encryption key managed by Couchbase Server. Do not assign an encryption key managed by a remote KMS to directly encrypt data.

notable_absence.finding: Within this single page, the same role is linked to roles.md under at least two different anchor spellings, and one role's anchor points at the WRONG role's section entirely. 'Full Admin' links to `roles.md#admin` three times (lines 63, 68->71, 80) but to `roles.md#full-admin` once (line 255) - two different anchors for one role on one page. More seriously, 'Bucket Admin' links to `roles.md#backup-full-admin` in the key-creation role list (line 77) but to the correct `roles.md#bucket-admin` in the bucket-encryption-enablement section (line 204) - the first of those two is a genuine wrong-target link, not just an inconsistent-but-valid spelling variant, since '#backup-full-admin' is Backup Full Admin's own anchor and 'Backup Full Admin' appears as ITS OWN separate bullet two lines above the mislinked Bucket Admin bullet. This is a concrete, fixable docs bug the extraction surfaces mechanically by simply keeping the exact anchor string as part of each requiresServerRole relation's evidence.

cross_component_finding: This page's three role-requirement groups (create a KEK-capable/audit-config-log key; create a key that can encrypt any bucket; create a key scoped to specific buckets) form a strict superset relationship - group 2 is group 1 plus Backup Full Admin/Cluster Admin/Eventing Full Admin, and group 3 is group 2 plus Bucket Admin - that the page states only through three separately-repeated bullet lists, never as an explicit hierarchy statement. The registry's role: family already carries several 'N structurally distinct roles' collision writeups; this page adds a data point for role:bucket-admin and role:security-admin specifically, both still sitting at the extraction layer despite recurring across several rounds now (learn/security/roles.md, this page), which is worth a look at promotion time.
cross_product_finding: n/a - no Capella/Mobile/SDK content on this page. Note, however, that the KMIP/AWS KMS integration warning ('these files must exist on every node in the cluster, including any nodes added during a rebalance operation... Couchbase Server does not create these files automatically') is a genuinely new admin-only, multi-node operational constraint with no equivalent statement anywhere else in the batch - worth flagging even though it does not fit cleanly into a two-concept relation: it is a precondition on cluster topology changes (rebalance) rather than on any single certificate or key object.
